q: How many looks does binary search need for 1,000,000 sorted items?
why: Each look drops half of what is left. I counted 20 for the worst case. Doubling the list adds one look.

q: In the exact-match shape, why do we write `lo = mid + 1` and not `lo = mid`?
options: It makes the search faster by one step
With `lo = mid` the area may not shrink and the loop can run for ever
why: With `[1, 2]` and target 2, `lo = mid` stays at 0 for ever. Every turn must make the search area smaller.
The lower bound is the first position where the value is at least the target. That is why it also gives "where to insert".

q: What makes "search the answer" (like the banana speed) possible?
options: A yes/no check that flips only once: no, no, no, yes, yes, yes
why: If "does speed k work?" flips once, we can binary search the speeds without any list.
With no comparer, `sort` turns the items into text. Use `(a, b) => a - b`.

q: How does merge sort work, and what does it cost?
options: Pick a pivot and swap: always O(n)
Split in half, sort each half, merge: O(n log n) time and O(n) extra space
Compare neighbours until no swap is left: O(n)
Count each value: O(n log n) with O(1) space
why: About log n levels of halving, and each level merges n items. The merged lists need extra memory.
